title: Datadog vs PagerDuty for incidents (and when to add Rootly)
summary: Datadog On-Call vs PagerDuty compared on paging, schedules, alert sources, status pages, retrospectives and pricing, plus when to add Rootly to either.
body_markdown:
**Short answer:** Datadog On-Call fits engineers already on Datadog who want monitors, paging and incidents on one bill. PagerDuty fits organizations with deep escalation chains and alerts from many tools beyond Datadog. Both handle layered schedules, escalation policies and overrides. Add Rootly when you want the incident itself run in Slack or Teams, from declaration to retrospective, on top of either.


**TL;DR:** These three tools are usually compared as if they do the same job. They do not. Datadog is where the signal starts, PagerDuty’s weight sits on getting a human to acknowledge, and Rootly is built around running the incident and learning from it. All three now reach into the others’ territory, so the useful question is less who *can* do what than where each one’s workflow actually lives. Most teams end up with two of the three; the question worth answering is which two, and who owns the seam between them.


## Datadog On-Call vs PagerDuty at a glance


Every cell links to the vendor’s own documentation or pricing page. Prices are list prices as published in October 2026.


Datadog On-Call PagerDuty


**Paging and escalation**[Escalation policies](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/escalation_policies/) of up to 10 steps, targeting schedules, users or teams, with notify-all or round robin.[Pages arrive](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/notification_preferences/) by push, SMS, phone call or email[Escalation policies](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/schedules/escalation-policies) of up to 20 rules, targeting users or schedules, with round robin and up to nine repeats


**Schedules**[Layered schedules](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/schedules/) with handoff times, business-hours conditions and overrides requested from Slack or Teams[Layered schedules](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/schedules/schedule-basics) with daily, weekly or custom rotations, restrictions and overrides


**Alert sources**[Datadog monitors, incidents, a team email address, Live Call Routing and manual pages](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/pages/) from Datadog, Slack or Teams[750+ platform integrations](https://www.pagerduty.com/integrations/) , Datadog among them


**Incident workflow**[Incident Management](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/incident_management/) , a separate product: declare incidents, open Slack or Teams channels, keep a timeline[Incident Workflows](https://docs.pagerduty.com/ai-automation/automation/incident-workflows) create Slack channels, Zoom meetings and status updates. Professional gets one workflow; Business and Enterprise up to 2,000


**Status pages**[Public or internal pages](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/status_pages/) with email and Slack subscribers[Internal, external and private status pages](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/communicate/status-pages-overview)


**Retrospectives**[Postmortems](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/incident_management/post_incident/postmortems/) filled from templates into Notebooks, Confluence or Google Drive[Post-Incident Reviews](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/after-incident/post-incident-reviews) with a narrative builder and AI drafts from Slack and the Scribe Agent


**Pricing model**[Per seat](https://www.datadoghq.com/pricing/list/) : On-Call $20 and Incident Management $30 per seat per month, billed annually[Per user](https://www.pagerduty.com/pricing/) : free for up to 5 users, Professional $21 per user per month billed annually, AIOps and status pages sold as add-ons


**Best fit** Engineers already consolidated on Datadog whose pages start from Datadog monitors Organizations with many alert sources, long escalation chains or an existing PagerDuty rollout


## When do teams choose PagerDuty over Datadog?


Teams choose PagerDuty over Datadog when paging has to cover more than Datadog: alerts from many monitoring tools and other systems, escalation chains longer than Datadog On-Call’s 10 steps, AIOps noise reduction, or an existing PagerDuty rollout they don’t want to rebuild. Datadog itself documents routing monitor alerts through existing PagerDuty services.


The five situations that come up most, each checkable on the vendors’ own pages:


1. **A multi-tool monitoring estate.** When Datadog is one of several monitoring tools, PagerDuty puts them behind one pager through its[750+ integrations](https://www.pagerduty.com/integrations/) . Datadog On-Call’s[documented page sources](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/pages/) are Datadog monitors and incidents, a team email address, Live Call Routing and manual pages.
2. **Complex escalation needs.** PagerDuty escalation policies allow[up to 20 rules, repeated up to nine times](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/schedules/escalation-policies) . Datadog On-Call allows[up to 10 steps of up to 10 targets each](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/escalation_policies/) . Teams whose escalation trees outgrow that limit stay on PagerDuty.
3. **AIOps.**[PagerDuty AIOps](https://www.pagerduty.com/platform/aiops/) correlates and deduplicates large volumes of incoming events before they page anyone. It is sold as an add-on on[PagerDuty’s pricing page](https://www.pagerduty.com/pricing/) , so budget for it separately.
4. **Existing contracts.** A team already paying for PagerDuty can keep it and point Datadog at it. Datadog’s[PagerDuty integration](https://docs.datadoghq.com/integrations/pagerduty/) routes monitor notifications and incident pages through existing PagerDuty services with an` @pagerduty-\[serviceName\]` handle.
5. **Non-Datadog alert sources.** PagerDuty’s[Events API v2](https://docs.pagerduty.com/developer/events-api-v2-overview) ingests events from monitoring tools and from other systems such as code repositories, automated workflow tools and configuration management. Teams that page on signals from outside observability use it as the common intake.


Rootly fits with either: it ingests Datadog monitor alerts and can page from them, and with PagerDuty it syncs services and opens Rootly incidents from PagerDuty alerts, so the incident runs in Slack or Microsoft Teams whichever tool sends the page.


## What each tool is actually for


Comparing these three as competitors obscures the useful distinction, which is where each one sits in the life of an incident.


Tool Where it sits What it owns Where it hands off


**Datadog** Detection Metrics, logs, traces, monitors, and the alert that fires Once the alert exists, someone has to be found


**PagerDuty** Notification On-call schedules, escalation policies, acknowledgement, paging reliability, and Incident Workflows that can open a Slack channel and post updates into it Response depth beyond those workflows, and the capabilities that sit above the base tier


**Rootly** Agentic response and learning Declaring the incident, roles, the channel, stakeholder updates, the timeline, the retrospective and its action items, AI across the entire lifecycle Feeds detection back: what was missing, what should alert differently


A team running all three is not over-buying. A team running one and expecting it to cover the other two is where the gaps show up.


## Why this comparison comes up now


Two changes made the boundaries blurry. Observability vendors moved downstream — Datadog now ships on-call and incident features, so the monitoring tool asks to be the paging tool. And paging vendors moved upstream, adding AIOps and response workflow on top of alerting.


The result is three products whose marketing pages overlap and whose day-to-day strengths still do not. The overlap is real but shallow: a bundled on-call feature is not the same product as a company whose whole business is paging reliability, and a workflow engine bolted onto a monitoring suite is not the same as one designed around how responders behave under pressure.


## How we evaluated


Criterion What we looked for


**Detection quality** Signal coverage, correlation, and how much noise reaches a human


**Paging reliability** Escalation behavior, delivery under failure, override handling


**Coordination** Channel and role automation, how little context-switching responders endure


**Post-incident** Timeline capture, retrospective workflow, whether action items are tracked to completion


**Chat nativeness** Whether the tool’s workflow lives inside Slack, Google Chat or Microsoft Teams, or reaches into them from its own app


**Commercial shape** How the tool is priced and what is an add-on rather than included


Everything below is checkable on each vendor’s own documentation.


## Datadog


Datadog’s strength is that the signal and its context live together. When an alert fires, the metric, the trace, the log line and the deploy that preceded it are one click apart. For teams already consolidated on Datadog, that is a genuine advantage no separate incident tool can reproduce.


**Where it fits:** teams whose reliability problem is mostly a detection problem, and whose response process is already working.


**Where it falls short:** coordination is not where its weight sits. Datadog does document incident management — roles, communication, timelines and retrospectives are all covered in its own docs — so the honest distinction is not that it cannot run an incident. It is that the response surface is the Datadog app with chat integration rather than the chat tool itself, and that the incident line is additive to a bill already scaling with hosts and data volume. The question to answer for your own team is whether responders will work where it asks them to.


## PagerDuty


PagerDuty is the most mature paging product in the category, and for the specific job of making sure a human acknowledges an urgent alert at 3am, it is good. Deep escalation policies, reliable delivery, a large integration catalog, and enough enterprise controls to survive procurement.


**Where it fits:** complex on-call structures at scale, especially where escalation rules are deep and legacy integrations matter.


**Where it falls short:** response depth relative to paging depth — and this one is easy to overstate, so precisely. PagerDuty’s Incident Workflows can create the incident Slack channel automatically and post status updates into it, and its Slack app can assign roles and add tasks without leaving chat. The difference is composition rather than capability: that response layer is configured on top of a paging product, and several of the capabilities that show up in comparisons, AIOps among them, are priced as add-ons above the base tier, so the quoted platform cost and the real cost often differ.


## Rootly


Rootly is built around the part of the incident that happens after someone acknowledges: declaring the incident, opening the channel, assigning the commander and scribe, paging the right secondary, posting stakeholder updates, capturing the timeline as it happens, and turning it into a retrospective with owned action items, with AI agents throughout the entire lifecycle to help automate the process.


Because that work happens in Slack, Google Chat or Microsoft Teams, Rootly runs there natively rather than notifying into it. On-call, response, AI investigations and root cause analysis, retrospectives and status pages are one platform, which is the difference between a timeline you have to assemble and one that is already written when the incident resolves.


**Where it fits:** teams that want the whole incident lifecycle in one place and want retrospectives to actually get done.


**Where it falls short:** Rootly is not an observability platform. If your problem is that you cannot see what is happening in production, you need Datadog or an equivalent first; Rootly consumes those signals rather than producing them.


## Choose Datadog On-Call if…, choose PagerDuty if…, add Rootly if…


### Choose Datadog On-Call if…


- Most of your pages start from a Datadog monitor, and you want the alert and its metrics, traces and logs one click apart.
- Your escalation fits in[10 steps of up to 10 targets each](https://docs.datadoghq.com/incident_response/on-call/escalation_policies/) .
- You would rather add on-call seats to the Datadog bill you already pay than sign another vendor.


### Choose PagerDuty if…


- Alerts come from many tools besides Datadog, and you want them in one pager. PagerDuty lists[750+ integrations](https://www.pagerduty.com/integrations/) .
- You need longer chains:[up to 20 escalation rules, repeated up to nine times](https://docs.pagerduty.com/incident-management/schedules/escalation-policies) .
- PagerDuty already runs on-call across many teams, and rebuilding those schedules is not on this year’s plan.


### Add Rootly if…


- You want responders to run the incident inside Slack, Microsoft Teams or Google Chat: the channel, roles, stakeholder updates and timeline, then a retrospective with tracked action items.
- **You run Datadog.** The[Rootly Datadog integration](https://docs.rootly.com/integrations/datadog/datadog) receives monitor alerts by webhook and routes them to on-call or incident workflows, pages a user, team, escalation policy or service straight from the alert payload, and pulls graph snapshots and dashboards into the incident. It is documented for Datadog monitors, not Datadog On-Call, so in a Datadog stack Rootly On-Call usually does the paging.
- **You run PagerDuty.** The[Rootly PagerDuty integration](https://docs.rootly.com/integrations/pagerduty/pagerduty) imports and syncs PagerDuty services, pages PagerDuty services, escalation policies and users from Rootly, creates Rootly incidents from PagerDuty alerts, and assigns incident roles from PagerDuty on-call schedules. PagerDuty keeps paging; Rootly runs the response.
- You want status pages included. Rootly Incident Response is $20 per user per month at list price and includes Status Pages; Rootly On-Call is another $20 if you later move paging too.


## The combinations teams actually run


If your stack is… The usual shape What to watch


Consolidated on Datadog, small team Datadog detection + Datadog On-Call Fewest moving parts; check whether your responders will run the incident in Datadog rather than in chat


Any observability + Slack or Teams culture Datadog + Rootly One fewer vendor; paging and response in the same platform


Large enterprise, complex escalation, existing PagerDuty contract Datadog + Rootly + PagerDuty Rootly runs the incident; PagerDuty keeps the paging tree it is good at, until you move paging to Rootly On-Call, which typically comes in at half the cost of PagerDuty


## Pricing shape, not price


Published numbers move, so compare the shape instead:


- **Datadog** is usage-based across products. Incident and on-call features are separate SKUs, so the incident line is additive to a bill that already scales with hosts and data volume.
- **PagerDuty** is tiered per user, with several of the capabilities that appear in comparisons — AIOps notably — sold as add-ons above the base tier.
- **Rootly** is per user and per product, and the products are additive. Incident Response is $20 per user per month and includes Status Pages; On-Call is another $20, so both together are $40. AI SRE is an add-on, priced separately and not sold standalone. What is *not* separately priced is the AI inside those products — the agent, similar incidents, scribe and retrospectives are part of Incident Response rather than a tier above it. Datadog and PagerDuty list prices from October 2026 are in the table at the top; check their pricing pages before you budget, because they change.


The question to ask any of the three: at our headcount, with the features we just demoed, what is the annual number? Feature lists compare badly; that number compares well.


## What about Opsgenie?


Opsgenie appears in many of these comparisons and should not be a candidate for new evaluations. Atlassian ended new sales on June 4, 2025 and ends support on **April 5, 2027** , so any Opsgenie decision today is a migration decision. If that is where you are, weigh migration tooling — schedules, escalation policies and integrations all have to survive the move.


## Key terms


Term What it means


**MTTA / MTTR** Mean time to acknowledge and to resolve — the two speed measures most teams report


**Escalation policy** The ordered rule for who gets paged next when nobody acknowledges


**AIOps** Applying machine learning to operations data, usually to correlate and compress alerts before a human sees them


**ChatOps** Running the incident from inside Slack or Microsoft Teams rather than a separate console


**Blameless retrospective** A post-incident review focused on systemic causes rather than individual fault


## Frequently asked questions


### Is Datadog On-Call cheaper than PagerDuty?


At list price, Datadog On-Call is $20 per seat per month billed annually and PagerDuty Professional is $21 per user per month billed annually. The bigger cost difference is elsewhere: Datadog Incident Management is a separate $30 seat, and PagerDuty sells AIOps and status pages as add-ons. Price the full stack you need.


### When do teams choose PagerDuty over Datadog?


Teams pick PagerDuty when alerts come from many tools besides Datadog, when escalation needs more than Datadog On-Call’s 10 steps, when they want AIOps noise reduction, or when a PagerDuty contract is already in place. Datadog monitors can route through existing PagerDuty services, so the two often run together. Rootly works with both and runs the incident itself in Slack or Teams.


### Can Datadog On-Call page from alerts outside Datadog?


Its documented page sources are Datadog monitors and incidents, a team email address, Live Call Routing and manual pages from Datadog, Slack or Teams. A tool that can send email can page through the team address. PagerDuty’s integration catalog is built for many outside sources.


### Does Rootly work with Datadog and PagerDuty?


Yes. Rootly ingests Datadog monitor alerts and can page from them, and it pulls Datadog graphs and dashboards into the incident. With PagerDuty, Rootly syncs services, pages PagerDuty escalation policies and opens Rootly incidents from PagerDuty alerts.


### Is Datadog a replacement for PagerDuty?


For simple on-call in a team already consolidated on Datadog, Datadog On-Call can cover the basics. For complex escalation across many teams, PagerDuty remains the more specialised product. The honest test is whether your escalation rules fit comfortably in the bundled feature.


### Do I need both PagerDuty and Rootly?


Not usually. Rootly includes on-call scheduling, escalation and paging, so most teams replace rather than stack. The exception is a large organization with an escalation tree it does not want to rebuild and an existing contract, where Rootly runs the incident and PagerDuty keeps paging.


### Which is best for Microsoft Teams?


Most of this category was built Slack-first. Rootly treats Microsoft Teams as a first-class surface rather than a notification target, which matters if Teams is where your responders actually work.


### What replaces Opsgenie?


Any of these three can, depending on which part of the job you need. Opsgenie support ends April 5, 2027, so treat it as a migration with a deadline rather than an option.


### Can any of these run a retrospective for me?


Rootly drafts one from the timeline it captured during the incident, and tracks the resulting action items to completion. Treat “AI-generated retrospective” claims from any vendor as a first draft, not a finished review — the analysis is the part a human still owns.
